results.title: ECOWAS wanted a reunion. The AES came to negotiate. On October 17 and 18, 2026, the two blocs sat at the same table in Dakar for the first t
results.description:
ECOWAS wanted a reunion. The AES came to negotiate.
 
On October 17 and 18, 2026, the two blocs sat at the same table in Dakar for the first time since Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger walked out of ECOWAS in January 2025. The room was full of foreign ministers. The air was full of speculation.
 
Then Burkina Faso's Foreign Minister, Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré, ended it with three words.
 
"Il n'en est rien." There is no truth in it.
 
He was answering the question that had been building for weeks: was the AES preparing to come back? The answer was no. Not now. Not like this.
 
The joint statement was careful. It spoke of "fraternity, mutual respect and openness." It stressed "good neighbourliness" and "respect for sovereignty." It announced working groups to prepare a framework cooperation agreement on trade, freedom of movement, and security.
 
What it did not announce was a reunion.
 
Mali's Abdoulaye Diop said the talks must be "entity-to-entity"—AES and ECOWAS as two separate organisations, not one bloc absorbing the other. Niger's Bakary Yaou Sangaré said it plainly: "The AES is not against ECOWAS, but it has another path."
 
That is what Dakar was. Not a homecoming. A negotiation between equals.
 
The AES did not leave ECOWAS to isolate itself. It left because the bloc sanctioned it, threatened it, and refused to accept that three sovereign states had chosen a different direction. In the 20 months since, the AES built a joint military force, an investment bank, and a common biometric passport. It did not need ECOWAS to survive. It does not need to rejoin to cooperate.
 
West Africa now has two regional bodies where there used to be one. The old bloc has to learn to share the room.
